title: Spiral Galaxy in the Coma Cluster, Part of a Larger Hubble Image
caption: Spiral galaxy IC 4040 in the Coma Cluster, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Coma Cluster, Abell 1656, IC 4040 · constellation Coma Berenices · about 300 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: This close-up, cut from a larger Hubble view of the Coma Cluster, shows a spiral galaxy cataloged as IC 4040. NASA's description of the full image singles out a bright spiral at upper left, brighter and bluer than its neighbors, with dusty spiral arms that look reddish brown against a whiter disc.

Those arms suggest that galaxy was disturbed at some point in the past. Bright, bluish-white spirals hold clouds of cold gas that are still forming new stars, and in Coma they are found away from the crowded center.

The cluster around it, also called Abell 1656, is one of the densest known collections of galaxies, with thousands of members spread through a sphere more than 20 million light-years across. Its central region is dominated by elliptical galaxies, featureless balls of old stars, both dwarf and giant. Between the two types sit S0 galaxies, made of older stars but showing some structure such as a bar or ring.

understand.summary: Cropped from a Hubble Advanced Camera for Surveys image of the Coma Cluster. The color mapping for this crop is not published.
understand.eye: The underlying image gathered about 12 hours of exposure, far more light than an eye could collect.

explore: Lying over 300 million light-years away in Coma Berenices, the cluster sits close to the Milky Way's north pole, where little dust from our own galaxy blocks the view. The larger image covers a section roughly one-third of the way out from the cluster's center.
